source.title: Universally Converging Representations of Matter Across Scientific Foundation Models
source.authors: Sathya Edamadaka; Soojung Yang; Ju Li; Rafael Gómez-Bombarelli

record.tranche_reason: The study applies CKNNA, the same representational similarity measure used in the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, to new scientific models and domains. It also reports additional metrics and analyses.
record.gate_note: The paper reports CKNNA and other alignment results across scientific models, performance-alignment trends, and results varying inputs and metrics. Individual values in the full alignment matrices and plots are not given in the text, so rows below preserve the explicitly stated aggregate trends rather than inventing pairwise values. Findings cited from other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study applies CKNNA (k=25), the Platonic Representation Hypothesis metric, to about 59 scientific models. It plots alignment to the best model against task performance, the same design as the original, in a new domain (materials, molecules, proteins). It adds dCor, information imbalance and a k sweep, which bear on V6 and V7. T3 would also fit, since the setting is new, but the method and measure follow the original.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that nearly sixty scientific models are substantially aligned across modalities and that MLIP representations converge as performance improves. They also find that current models are data-limited: in distribution, representations cluster by training dataset; out of distribution, they collapse onto low-information, architecture-specific manifolds. They propose alignment to other strong models as a benchmark for foundational generality.
record.recipe_differences: Uses CKNNA as in the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, applied to scientific foundation models and matter datasets; supplements it with dCor, intrinsic dimensionality, and information imbalance.
record.method_sensitivity: CKNNA score increases as k changes from 2 to 2500, although alignment ordering is mostly consistent. The reported relationship also varies with input dataset and with whether the metric is local or global.

fits_no_version.finding: String-based, LLM and protein sequence models align with 3D-coordinate or structure models across modalities.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scientific models with different input modalities of the same matter have nontrivially aligned representations.

fits_no_version.finding: Intrinsic dimensionality falls in a narrow, dataset-specific band across architectures; invariant embeddings have lower Id than equivariant or vanilla ones (Fig. 1E).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Independently trained models share similar latent complexity (intrinsic dimension) on the same inputs.

fits_no_version.finding: Orb V3 conservative models (trained with equigrad regularization) align with equivariant architectures, while Orb V3 direct models align weakly (Fig. 1A, Sec. 3.3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training regularizers that impose a symmetry produce representations similar to those of architectures that build the symmetry in.

record.code_released: https://github.com/learningmatter-mit (the paper says code will soon be available)
record.problems: The supplied text does not give most individual pairwise alignment values or uncertainty estimates; many results are conveyed through figures and qualitative descriptions. The paper's performance-alignment results concern particular scientific datasets and model families, not a general cross-domain scale law.
record.rows_left_out: Individual pairwise values from the full CKNNA matrices and plotted model points are not transcribed because the supplied text gives them only in figures, without readable numeric values or a textual result for each pair. The relevant plots and matrices are identified in the row locators.

untested.parts: Scale is tested only through energy-regression performance in materials and QM9 sweeps. There is no direct parameter-count trend, and the results do not carry beyond scientific models.
There are no vision or language models of paired image–caption data.
There are no comparisons across random seeds.
There are no mappings, stitching, relative representations or unpaired translation.
There are no neuron, SAE-feature or circuit comparisons.
Only CKNNA k, dCor, information imbalance, Id Cor and dataset choice are varied. There is no broad sweep over similarity measures.
There is no plateau analysis, and the effect of shared objectives is not separated from that of shared data.

missing.what: QM9 information imbalance: models trained on the same dataset almost always learn identical information, while those trained on different datasets often learn orthogonal information.
The evolutionary tree groups models by dataset before architecture; MACE-OFF diverges from MACE-MP despite a similar architecture.
Id Cor agrees less with information imbalance than CKNNA and dCor do, so the alignment picture depends on the metric.
Information imbalance becomes more orthogonal as k increases.
Models of the same family but very different sizes learn very similar representations, with only slight performance differences.

record.verdict_notes: Most values are available only in figures, and no uncertainty is reported. R9's out-of-distribution collapse, where poor models are highly aligned, also qualifies V1: alignment can arise without capability. It is labelled under V7 only because a row carries a single state. Fig. 3 uses dCor, not CKNNA, because the authors judged QM9 out of distribution for most of the models.

versions.untested_parts: Does not establish a general trend for all architectures, objectives, data, or modalities; performance-alignment sweeps concern scientific models and the reported materials and small-molecule settings.
No paired image-caption vision/language models or test of alignment increasing as both models improve.
No comparison of networks trained from different random initializations to identify shared features or subspaces.
No mapping between representations, stitching, relative-representation test, or unpaired translation.
No test of recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits.
Tests CKNNA locality settings, multiple similarity measures, and input datasets; does not report a broad sweep over all reasonable similarity measures or all out-of-distribution settings.
Reports incomplete alignment and training-data effects in the tested scientific models, but does not establish a numerical plateau or isolate shared objectives from shared training data.

rows.subject: Materials models in Fig. 1B (aggregate trend)
rows.size_stated: Model sizes vary; individual sizes are not stated in the text for this result.
rows.operation_detail: Compared energy-regression MAE on OMat24 with CKNNA alignment to UMA Medium.
rows.measure: CKNNA alignment to the best-performing model versus energy-regression MAE
rows.value: The text reports that alignment to UMA Medium increases as models improve at energy prediction.
rows.note: The figure plots individual models, but the text reports the trend rather than their individual values.

rows.subject: EqV2 OMPA and EqV2 OMat model families (aggregate trend)
rows.size_stated: Small, Medium, and Large variants are listed in Table 1.
rows.operation_detail: Compared representation alignment across family variants as size and performance increase.
rows.value: The text reports that the family variants become more aligned as they increase in size and performance.
rows.note: The text describes the within-family trend; individual pairwise scores are not transcribed.

rows.subject: Scientific models evaluated on QM9 (aggregate trend)
rows.size_stated: Varies; individual sizes are not stated in the text for this result.
rows.operation_detail: Compared small-molecule energy-regression MAE with distance-correlation alignment to the best-performing model.
rows.measure: dCor alignment to Orb V3 Conservative Inf MP versus energy-regression MAE
rows.value: The text reports that alignment to the reference increases as models' energy-regression MAE decreases.
rows.note: The trend is described in the text; per-model plotted values are not given.

rows.subject: MACE-OFF model
rows.size_stated: Large, Medium, and Small variants are listed in Table 1; the text does not identify which plotted variant is meant here.
rows.operation_detail: Compared alignment with high-performing models despite strong QM9 performance.

conditions.value: Orb V3 family, UMA, and other high-performing models

rows.baseline: Alignment of other high-performing models, not numerically stated
rows.value: The text reports strong QM9 performance but weak alignment to Orb V3, UMA, and other high-performing models.
rows.note: The authors interpret this as a local optimum and suggest reduced transferability beyond QM9's chemical space.
rows.check: For V1 this is a counterexample, not a weaker effect. MACE-OFF performs strongly on QM9 yet is weakly aligned with the other high-performing models, so capability does not bring alignment for this model. The V7 link is dropped: the authors attribute it to a local optimum, not to shared data or objectives.

rows.subject: Pairs of scientific model representations on small molecules (aggregate comparison)
rows.operation_detail: Compared local CKNNA with global distance correlation.
rows.measure: Agreement between CKNNA and dCor across model pairs
rows.value: The text reports that CKNNA is highly correlated with dCor.
rows.note: This weighs against the claim that the observed alignment trend is only a local-metric artifact.

rows.subject: Scientific model pairs on sAlex (aggregate comparison)
rows.operation_detail: Swept the nearest-neighbor parameter k used by CKNNA.
rows.measure: CKNNA score and ordering of model alignments
rows.value: CKNNA increases monotonically with k; the ordering of model alignments is described as mostly consistent across k.
rows.note: The metric's magnitudes vary with k, while the reported ordering is mostly preserved.
rows.check: The Fig. A1 caption says ordering is preserved 'almost exactly' as k goes from 2 to 2500. Only the absolute CKNNA magnitude rises. The k choice therefore does not weaken or remove the measured convergence pattern, and partial overstates the dependence.

source_check.correct: state=partial for V6: absolute CKNNA scores increase monotonically with k, while model-alignment ordering remains almost unchanged.
source_check.problem: Absent overlooks the explicitly observed dependence of absolute alignment scores on neighbour count.

rows.subject: Scientific model pairs on OMat24 and OMol25 (aggregate comparison)
rows.operation_detail: Compared representation relationships for in-distribution and out-of-distribution structures using local and global measures.
rows.measure: Alignment and information overlap between model representations
rows.baseline: OMat24 in-distribution results compared with OMol25 out-of-distribution results
rows.value: Local alignment is reported as higher for in-distribution structures, while global alignment by information imbalance and dCor is reported as higher for out-of-distribution structures.
rows.note: The direction depends on whether local or global alignment is considered and on the input dataset.
rows.check: The local-versus-global and in- versus out-of-distribution contrast is a metric and input dependence, so it belongs to V6, where it is observed. The V7 link is unsupported because the row does not concern completeness of alignment or its causes.

rows.subject: Weakly performing models on in-distribution materials (aggregate result)
rows.operation_detail: Measured information imbalance among model embeddings.
rows.value: The text reports weak alignment and nearly orthogonal information among weakly performing models, consistent with divergent local sub-optima.
rows.note: The stated result concerns the weakly performing subset, not every model.
rows.check: Weak in-distribution models being weakly aligned, with nearly orthogonal information, is the low-performance side of V1's performance–alignment link. It does not show alignment being explained by shared data, so it is relinked from V7 to V1.

rows.subject: Models evaluated on OMol25 (aggregate result)
rows.operation_detail: Measured information imbalance and representation alignment on out-of-distribution structures.
rows.measure: Information imbalance and similarity of represented information
rows.value: The text reports that nearly all models perform poorly on OMol25 but represent nearly identical, low-information content; models cluster by architecture.
rows.note: The authors describe this as a collapse onto architecture-specific manifolds that omit information needed for complex structures.
rows.check: Out of distribution, poorly performing models represent nearly identical low-information content and cluster by architecture. Alignment here comes from architectural bias, not shared capability. This also qualifies V1 (alignment without performance), noted under V7 because the row has a single state.

rows.subject: eSEN and EqV2 model pairs (aggregate comparison)
rows.operation_detail: Compared alignment by training dataset and architecture.

conditions.value: eSEN and EqV2 models trained on OMat24 versus eSEN trained on MPTraj

rows.baseline: eSEN OMat24 compared with eSEN MPTraj
rows.value: The text reports that eSEN models trained on OMat24 align more closely with EqV2 models trained on OMat24 than with eSEN models trained on MPTraj.
rows.note: The authors use this example to argue that, in-distribution, training data can shape representations more strongly than architecture.

rows.subject: String-based molecular models and Orb architectures (aggregate comparison)
rows.operation_detail: Compared representations from string-encoded molecules and 3D atom-coordinate models.
rows.value: The text reports nontrivial alignment between string-based models and atomistic MLIPs, particularly between SMILES-based models and Orb architectures; these cross-modal values exceed the highest vision-language alignment values cited by the authors.
rows.note: This is cross-modal scientific-model alignment, but it does not test whether alignment rises as both models improve.
rows.check: The comparison saying these values exceed the vision-language values is against results cited from the original PRH paper, not measured here. String-versus-3D alignment is not V2's image–caption pairing, and the row has no performance trend.

rows.subject: DeepSeek R1, Qwen3 30B A3B Thinking 2507, and GPT OSS 20B (aggregate comparison)
rows.size_stated: Sizes are listed in Table 1; the text does not assign separate alignment results to individual models here.
rows.operation_detail: Compared language-model representations of SMILES inputs with scientific model representations.

conditions.value: The paper includes extended and blank variants

rows.measure: Alignment of LLM representations with string-based models and MLIPs
rows.value: The text reports strong alignment with string-encoding-based materials models when given SMILES strings, and alignment scores with MLIPs similar to those of other SMILES-based models.
rows.note: The main text does not break this reported outcome down by LLM or system-prompt variant.

rows.subject: Protein sequence and structure models (aggregate comparison)
rows.operation_detail: Compared representations from protein sequence and protein structure models.

conditions.value: RCSB protein structures and associated sequences

rows.baseline: Best small-molecule cases, as described by the authors
rows.value: The text reports that sequence-model and structure-model representations align nearly twice as strongly as the best small-molecule cases.
rows.note: This is scientific protein sequence/structure alignment, not the vision-language paired image-caption test in V2.

rows.subject: Random Baseline
rows.operation_detail: Included a random representation baseline in the alignment analysis.
rows.note: The figure caption says a random baseline was included, but the supplied text does not state its result.
rows.check: This is a control whose values appear only in the figure. It is not itself a test of any version.

relationships.condition: In-distribution OMat24 materials models (CKNNA) and QM9 models (dCor), across and within the EqV2 families
relationships.reason: Alignment to the best model (UMA Medium; Orb V3 Conservative) rises as energy MAE falls, and weak models diverge (R1, R2, R3, R8).
relationships.display_finding: Alignment with UMA Medium or Orb V3 Conservative increased as energy MAE decreased, while weaker models diverged.

source_check.reason: R1–R3 report increasing alignment with improving performance, including within EqV2 families; R8 supplies the weak-performance counterpart.

relationships.reason: A high-performing model stays weakly aligned with the other strong models, so performance does not guarantee convergence (R4).
relationships.display_finding: MACE-OFF achieved strong performance on QM9 while remaining weakly aligned with other high-performing models.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: R4 and Section 2.2.1 explicitly identify strong performance with weak alignment as an exception; for this condition the predicted performance–alignment effect is absent.

relationships.condition: In-distribution OMat24 versus out-of-distribution OMol25 inputs, local versus global measures
relationships.reason: Which inputs are used flips whether local or global alignment is higher, so measured convergence depends on metric and data (R7).
relationships.display_finding: Switching from OMat24 to out-of-distribution OMol25 reversed the ordering of local and global alignment.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: In-distribution OMat24 versus out-of-distribution OMol25 inputs, local versus global measures
source_check.reason: R7 shows higher local alignment in distribution but higher global alignment out of distribution, establishing dependence on metric and inputs.

relationships.condition: CKNNA versus dCor on small molecules; CKNNA k swept from 2 to 2500 on sAlex
relationships.reason: CKNNA correlates highly with dCor, and model ordering is preserved almost exactly across k; only magnitudes shift (R5, R6).
relationships.display_finding: CKNNA correlated highly with dCor, and model ordering was almost unchanged as k ranged from 2 to 2500, although absolute scores shifted.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: CKNNA versus dCor on small molecules; CKNNA k swept from 2 to 2500 on sAlex
source_check.reason: R5 supports agreement across metrics and R6 preserves ordering, but R6 also explicitly changes absolute scores with k. These results qualify weakening or disappearance without establishing absent metric-setting dependence.

relationships.condition: OMat24 training-data comparisons and out-of-distribution OMol25
relationships.reason: Shared training data aligns different architectures more than a shared architecture does. Out of distribution, alignment reflects architecture bias and missing information, not shared capability (R9, R10).
relationships.display_finding: Shared training data aligned different architectures more than shared architecture did; out-of-distribution alignment reflected architectural bias and information availability rather than shared capability.

source_check.reason: R10 associates alignment more strongly with shared training data than architecture; R9 identifies similar incomplete information and architecture-specific collapse despite poor performance.

relation.reason: Its own representation, performance, metric-sensitivity and distribution comparisons directly test the claim versions.

tranche.reason: The study applies the original CKNNA measure and compares alignment with model performance; additional metrics and a scientific domain supplement that test.

source_check.notes: Code release is promised, not documented as completed. OMat24 energy MAE explicitly uses 1,000 structures; general alignment analyses use 50,000, and Fig. 1B's alignment sample size is not separately specified.

statements.correction: MACE-OFF: strong QM9 performance; weak alignment with Orb V3, UMA and other high-performing models; explicit exception in Section 2.2.1; V1 challenges for this condition.
statements.problem: The MACE-OFF finding is accurate, but its condition-specific absent performance–alignment effect warrants challenges under the verdict rules.

statements.correction: sAlex; k=2,25,50,100,1000,2500; CKNNA increases monotonically; ordering preserved almost exactly; robustness concerns ordering, with score dependence retained.
statements.problem: The ordering claim is accurate, but the challenges label overlooks simultaneous dependence of absolute scores on k.

statements.correction: OMat24-trained eSEN aligns more closely with OMat24-trained EqV2 than with MPTraj-trained eSEN; Code Availability promises a future release on Learning Matter GitHub.
statements.problem: The training-data comparison is correct; the header's affirmative code status is stronger than the paper's prospective release statement.
